full_judgment:
Ranadhir Sen J.—This Rule at the instance of the pre-emptee is directed against a judgment of reversal in a proceedings under section 76 of the State Acquisition and tenancy Act. 

 7. On consideration of the principles on which the above decisions rest, if may be stated that these principles have no manner of application to a right of pre-emption based on a statute. As already observed, in the aforesaid decisions of the Allahabad High Court, the right was based on a contract or village custom and their Lordships while searching for the genesis of the right, observed that it was due to "influence of the Muhammadan Law" and as such in assertion of the said right, the principle of justice, equity and good conscience was applied in the background of the principles laid down on Muhammadan Law relating to the right of pre-emption. In the instant case, the right of pre-emption is a creature of the statute and is not based on a village contract or custom. Accordingly the principles of justice and equity of good conscience cannot be applied. In section 96 (11) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act clear reservations have been made on that behalf viz., "Nothing in this section shall take away the right of pre-emption conferred on any person by the Muhammadan Law". The legislature therefore, clearly intended to keep the right of pre-emption conferred on a person by the Muhammadan Law separated from the right created under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In the circumstances, it must be held that the right of preemption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is a statutory right and is to be exercised within the scope of the statute itself. There is no embargo in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act that the right of pre-emption shall stand forfeited if a disqualified person is joined with the pre-emptor in an application for pre-emption. It has been held in the case of Matilal Sikdar Vs. Menodini 28 DLR (Appl. Divn.) 5 that the benefit conferred under the said provision is meant for certain individuals. The preconditions enabling the pre-emptor to exercise the right of pre-emption have been clearly stated in section 96(1) of the Act Section 96(2) of the act prescribes the persons who are to be impleaded. In the circumstances the contention of Mr. Abu Taher Chowdhury that pre-emptor No. 2, the husband associating himself with pre-emptor No.1, the wife forfeited his right of pre-emption under section 96 of the Act is clearly misconceived and is of no substance. 

 8. Mr. Chowdhury has next made a twofold grievance with regard to the deposit jointly made by the husband and wife once, at the time of making the application for pre-emption and then before the appellate court in respect of the costs of the improvement. Mr. Chowdhury failed to cite any authority in support of his view that the deposit vitiated the right of the pre-emptor No. 2. There is nothing in the statute to indicate that a joint deposit frustrates a right of pre-emption. In the case of Abdul Malek Laskar Vs. Begum Tayabnnnessa and others, (1966) 18 DLR 18, the question of joint deposit was noticed and it was held that the correct position in law with regard to joint deposit is that same sum of money in being deposited by both or either of them jointly. No objection can be taken by the petitioner on the ground that the money was deposited by the husband and the wife jointly. He is merely concerned with the deposit and joint deposit means what we have stated above. It does not mean that the husband deposited half the amount and wife had deposited the other half. Both have deposited the same amount jointly and separately. The learned District Judge considered the question of joint deposit in accordance with the view expressed above and correctly held that the deposit was valid. For the same reasons, the joint deposit of Tk. 700/- made before the appellate court must be held valid. Therefore, the joint deposit did not vitiate the pre-emption. 

 For the reasons stated above the Rule is discharged with costs assessed at 5 (five) gold Mohars. Send down the records at once.
